text: Lakoff holds that conventional ('dead') metaphors are used constantly and automatically, without effort or awareness, yet still structure thought; his 1986 paper title 'The Death of Dead Metaphor' rejects the inert view. (medium confidence)

text: Career-of-metaphor theory: novel metaphors are processed by comparison, and with repeated use the base term gains a domain-general category sense, so processing shifts to categorization and gets faster. This gives a mechanism for deadness as a gradient. (medium confidence)

text: Because deadness is relative to reader and context, extending a dead engineering metaphor literally (for example, a bug that 'crawls') can revive its imagery; this is the point where dead metaphors start to collide. (low confidence)

text: Scholars disagree on whether dead metaphors are dead: Max Black treats them as separate vocabulary items rather than metaphors, while R.W. Gibbs argues they retain metaphorical qualities, and Turbayne and Walton argue they keep influencing thought. (medium confidence)

text: Orwell distinguishes a dead metaphor, one that has reverted to being an ordinary word, from a dying metaphor, one that has lost evocative power and is used without knowledge of its meaning; he objects to the dying kind, not the dead kind. (medium confidence)

text: Software bug and thinking-machine constructs such as if/then, call/return and while are cited as dead metaphors in engineering language; readers no longer picture a cockroach. (low confidence)
